      file: 01-eap-chemical.pdf
      kind: program · status: gaps_found · shown as: needs_work

      what the reading said it is: This is your written plan for what employees do in a fire, chemical release, medical emergency or earthquake at the Portland facility. It is your own document, so you can fix it. In Oregon it is checked against Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule, OAR 437-002-0042. It covers evacuation, headcounts, first aid, alarm signals, designated wardens and reviews with employees. It leaves out three things the rule requires: how to report an emergency, how to shut down critical equipment before leaving, and who employees contact about the plan. It was last revised in February 2021 and shows no review since.
      WHAT THE READING FOUND WRONG WITH IT (7) — these are already findings; carry them, do not re-find them:
        · No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
            The plan says pull stations are at each exit and that an outside company monitors the alarm. It never says who calls 911, how to report a chemical release or medical emergency that won't set off the fire alarm, or which phone numbers to use.
            what it needs: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. It should say: pull the nearest station for a fire; call 911 from a safe place for any fire, release or serious injury; tell the incident coordinator or a supervisor; and give the site address to give the dispatcher. List the internal phone numbers.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(c)
        · No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
            The rule requires procedures for emergency operation or shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation. The plan tells everyone to leave at once. The only shutdown it mentions is the ventilation shutoff during shelter-in-place. For a chemical manufacturer with a laboratory, there is nothing on reactors, heating, transfer pumps, gas cylinders or other process equipment, and nothing saying who, if anyone, stays behind to do it.
            what it needs: Decide which equipment must be made safe before people leave. Name the job title responsible, write the steps and a cut-off point after which that person leaves too. If nothing needs a shutdown, say so in writing.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(d)
        · No named contact for questions about the plan; incident coordinator not identified
            The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about their duties under the plan. No one is named for this. The plan also relies on an 'incident coordinator' but never says who holds that role or who stands in when that person is absent.
            what it needs: Add a contacts section. Give the job title, and ideally the name and phone number, of the plan contact (for example the facilities lead), the incident coordinator and a backup.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(f)
        · Earthquake listed in scope but no earthquake procedure  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            Section 1 lists earthquakes as a covered emergency. The plan only gives procedures for alarm-triggered evacuation and shelter-in-place. It doesn't say what to do during and right after shaking (drop, cover and hold on, then evacuate once shaking stops and check for chemical spills). The rule asks for the 'type of evacuation' for each emergency. Whether that means a separate earthquake procedure is required is my reading, not a checked requirement.
            what it needs: Add a short earthquake procedure. Cover what to do during shaking, when to evacuate, which routes to avoid (the freight lift, racking, the lab), and a post-quake check for chemical spills and gas leaks.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) (my reading)
        · No statement on how far employees respond to chemical spills  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            The plan covers chemical releases by evacuating or sheltering in place. It doesn't say whether employees clean up small spills themselves (incidental releases) or never respond. If employees do respond beyond small incidental spills, the federal hazardous waste and emergency response rule (HAZWOPER, 29 CFR 1910.120(q)) would require a separate emergency response plan and training. I'm not sure how Oregon has adopted this; I believe it is by reference.
            what it needs: Add a sentence saying employees do not respond to chemical releases beyond small incidental spills they are trained to clean up, and that larger releases are handled by the fire department. If that isn't true, a separate HAZWOPER emergency response plan is needed.
            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.120(q) (not confirmed for how Oregon applies it)
        · Appendices A and B are not in the file
            The plan points to evacuation maps (Appendix A) and to the floor warden and first-aid responder roster (Appendix B) for exit route assignments and designated evacuation helpers. Neither is attached. So there is no way to check that exit routes are assigned or that designated employees exist, which the rule requires.
            what it needs: Attach the current evacuation maps and the current warden and first-aid roster to the plan, with dates. Check that the roster names people who still work there.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) and (4)
        · The plan's own January review has not been recorded since 2021  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            The plan commits to a review every January, but the revision date is still February 2021 and there is no review log or sign-off. This is the plan's own commitment, not a specific Oregon rule.
            what it needs: Add a review log at the end (date, reviewer, changes made). Carry out and record a review now.
            the rule: none (the plan's own commitment)
      DATES THIS DOCUMENT SETS (4):
        · Annual January review of the plan by the facilities lead — 2027-01-31 (recurring)
        · Annual training for floor wardens and first-aid responders — no date stated (recurring)
        · Autumn evacuation drill (twice a year, spring and autumn) — no date stated (recurring)
        · Monthly fire alarm test by the facilities lead — 2026-10-05 (recurring)
      WHAT THE READING SAID A COMPANY LIKE THIS USUALLY ALSO HOLDS (8) —
        a suggestion from similar companies, NOT a checked requirement:
        · Chemical Hygiene Plan for the laboratory — The plan shows laboratory staff are on site.
        · Fire Prevention Plan (OAR 437-002-0043) — Workplaces where everyone evacuates in a fire usually need one alongside the emergency action plan.
        · Hazard Communication program, SDS library and chemical inventory — A chemical manufacturer's employees handle hazardous chemicals every day.
        · Hazardous substance inventory reporting (EPCRA Tier II / Oregon State Fire Marshal Hazardous Substance Information Survey) — Commonly required for facilities that store chemicals above reporting thresholds.
        · Hazardous waste generator documents and contingency plan; spill plan (SPCC) or Oregon integrated contingency plan — Chemical manufacturers commonly generate hazardous waste and store oil or chemicals in bulk.
        · Oregon safety committee records (OAR 437-001-0765) — Oregon employers with more than 10 employees usually keep safety committee minutes.
        · OSHA 300/300A injury logs — Commonly kept by manufacturers with more than 10 employees.
        · Records of evacuation drills, alarm tests and warden/first-aid training — The plan promises drills twice a year, monthly alarm tests and annual training; the records are what show these happened.
      WHAT THIS DOCUMENT SAYS, proposed by the reading, not confirmed by anyone (5):
        · emergency eyewash shower location: Emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock; AED and first-aid kit in the front office, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely"
            where: Section 5, page 4
        · employees evacuate during fire: All employees evacuate when the fire alarm sounds; the plan gives no role for employees in fighting fires, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit."
            where: Section 3, page 3
        · employs drivers: The Portland workforce includes drivers, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff"
            where: Section 1, page 2
        · fire alarm monitoring vendor: Fire alarm monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract."
            where: Section 2, page 2
        · onsite laboratory: The Portland facility has a laboratory with laboratory staff, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall."
            where: Section 3, page 3

            There are no entries for Thursday Sep 3 or Friday Sep 4. The hour meter goes from 4,819 (start of shift Sep 2) to 4,834 (Sep 7). That is about 15 hours, but the Sep 2 shift explains only about 7 of them. This suggests the truck ran about one more shift with no pre-shift inspection written down.
            what it needs: Ask the operators and supervisor whether FL-2 was used on Sep 3 or 4. If it was, write a dated note on the log explaining the missing inspection, and remind operators that every shift of use needs an entry first.
            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) (examined before being placed in service, at least daily), which Oregon OSHA enforces through its Division 2 general industry rules. I have not confirmed the exact Oregon rule number.

      what the reading said it is: This is the company's own yearly summary of work-related injuries and illnesses at the Portland facility for 2025, filled in on the federal OSHA 300A form and signed by the Plant Manager on February 1, 2026 (page 1). It shows 3 recordable injuries: 1 with 6 days away from work and 2 other recordable cases. There were no deaths and no job-transfer or restriction cases. It is a record, so it was checked for completeness and for whether it fits with what the company has already confirmed. It was not checked against a program standard.
      WHAT THE READING FOUND WRONG WITH IT (3) — these are already findings; carry them, do not re-find them:
        · Annual average employee count does not match the confirmed headcount  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            The form reports an annual average of 65 employees and 128,400 hours worked in 2025. The company has confirmed 42 employees at Portland. 128,400 hours works out to about 1,975 hours per person for 65 people, which is plausible. For 42 people it would be about 3,057 hours each, which is not. So either headcount dropped after 2025, the figure counts temporary or leased workers, or one of the numbers is wrong. The 2025 average also affects whether the 20-employee threshold for electronic filing applies to the site.

documents.title: Emergency Action Plan – Portland Facility
documents.summary: This is your written plan for what employees do in a fire, chemical release, medical emergency or earthquake at the Portland facility. It is your own document, so you can fix it. In Oregon it is checked against Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule, OAR 437-002-0042. It covers evacuation, headcounts, first aid, alarm signals, designated wardens and reviews with employees. It leaves out three things the rule requires: how to report an emergency, how to shut down critical equipment before leaving, and who employees contact about the plan. It was last revised in February 2021 and shows no review since.

open_gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
open_gaps.description: The plan says pull stations are at each exit and that an outside company monitors the alarm. It never says who calls 911, how to report a chemical release or medical emergency that won't set off the fire alarm, or which phone numbers to use.
open_gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. It should say: pull the nearest station for a fire; call 911 from a safe place for any fire, release or serious injury; tell the incident coordinator or a supervisor; and give the site address to give the dispatcher. List the internal phone numbers.

open_gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
open_gaps.description: The rule requires procedures for emergency operation or shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation. The plan tells everyone to leave at once. The only shutdown it mentions is the ventilation shutoff during shelter-in-place. For a chemical manufacturer with a laboratory, there is nothing on reactors, heating, transfer pumps, gas cylinders or other process equipment, and nothing saying who, if anyone, stays behind to do it.
open_gaps.fix: Decide which equipment must be made safe before people leave. Name the job title responsible, write the steps and a cut-off point after which that person leaves too. If nothing needs a shutdown, say so in writing.

open_gaps.title: No named contact for questions about the plan; incident coordinator not identified
open_gaps.description: The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about their duties under the plan. No one is named for this. The plan also relies on an 'incident coordinator' but never says who holds that role or who stands in when that person is absent.
open_gaps.fix: Add a contacts section. Give the job title, and ideally the name and phone number, of the plan contact (for example the facilities lead), the incident coordinator and a backup.

open_gaps.title: Earthquake listed in scope but no earthquake procedure
open_gaps.description: Section 1 lists earthquakes as a covered emergency. The plan only gives procedures for alarm-triggered evacuation and shelter-in-place. It doesn't say what to do during and right after shaking (drop, cover and hold on, then evacuate once shaking stops and check for chemical spills). The rule asks for the 'type of evacuation' for each emergency. Whether that means a separate earthquake procedure is required is my reading, not a checked requirement.
open_gaps.fix: Add a short earthquake procedure. Cover what to do during shaking, when to evacuate, which routes to avoid (the freight lift, racking, the lab), and a post-quake check for chemical spills and gas leaks.

open_gaps.title: No statement on how far employees respond to chemical spills
open_gaps.description: The plan covers chemical releases by evacuating or sheltering in place. It doesn't say whether employees clean up small spills themselves (incidental releases) or never respond. If employees do respond beyond small incidental spills, the federal hazardous waste and emergency response rule (HAZWOPER, 29 CFR 1910.120(q)) would require a separate emergency response plan and training. I'm not sure how Oregon has adopted this; I believe it is by reference.
open_gaps.fix: Add a sentence saying employees do not respond to chemical releases beyond small incidental spills they are trained to clean up, and that larger releases are handled by the fire department. If that isn't true, a separate HAZWOPER emergency response plan is needed.
open_gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q) (not confirmed for how Oregon applies it)

open_gaps.title: Appendices A and B are not in the file
open_gaps.description: The plan points to evacuation maps (Appendix A) and to the floor warden and first-aid responder roster (Appendix B) for exit route assignments and designated evacuation helpers. Neither is attached. So there is no way to check that exit routes are assigned or that designated employees exist, which the rule requires.
open_gaps.fix: Attach the current evacuation maps and the current warden and first-aid roster to the plan, with dates. Check that the roster names people who still work there.

open_gaps.description: The plan commits to a review every January, but the revision date is still February 2021 and there is no review log or sign-off. This is the plan's own commitment, not a specific Oregon rule.

findings.title: Emergency action plan missing required procedures for reporting emergencies
findings.locator: Section 2 and 3, pages 2–3
findings.what_to_do: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section to the plan. It should state: pull the nearest alarm station for a fire; call 911 from a safe place for any fire, release or serious injury; tell the incident coordinator or a supervisor; and give the site address to the dispatcher. List the internal phone numbers.

findings.title: Emergency action plan missing procedures for shutting down critical equipment before evacuation
findings.locator: Section 3, page 3
findings.quote: When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit.
findings.what_to_do: Decide which equipment must be made safe before people leave (reactors, heating, transfer pumps, gas cylinders, process equipment). findings.title: Emergency action plan missing named contact for plan information and incident coordinator identification

findings.title: Emergency action plan covers earthquakes but provides no earthquake procedure

findings.title: Emergency action plan does not state the scope of employee response to chemical spills
